subtopic: Free bodyweight and machine training for runners

claims.topic: Free weights and bodyweight versus machines
claims.claim: Multi-joint free-weight and bodyweight exercises are likely to transfer to running better than machine-only or single-joint work, because they demand more coordination and multi-planar control and sit closer to the running action.
claims.evidence: A systematic review of strength training for middle- and long-distance runners argues that multi-joint free-weight exercises provide a superior neuromuscular stimulus and greater specificity to running than machine-based or single-joint work, which may explain the absence of benefit in studies that used only machines.

citation.title: Effects of Strength Training on the Physiological Determinants of Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review
citation.authors: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR

claims.topic: Matched-load adaptations: free weight versus machine
claims.claim: When the load and effort are matched, free-weight and machine-based training produce broadly similar gains in strength and muscle size, so the choice is more about specificity, balance and preference than about one being clearly superior.
claims.evidence: Using velocity-based methods, a longitudinal study found that adaptations in performance and muscle architecture were not meaningfully different between free-weight and machine-based training.

citation.title: Adaptations in athletic performance and muscle architecture are not meaningfully conditioned by training free-weight versus machine-based exercises
citation.authors: Hernandez-Belmonte A, Buendia-Romero A, Franco-Lopez F, Martinez-Cava A, Pallares JG

claims.claim: Lower-limb resistance training improves running economy and performance, and lowers running-related injury risk, so a small amount of strength work belongs in most running plans.
claims.evidence: A narrative review reports robust evidence that lower-limb resistance exercise improves running economy and biomechanics, and recommends a mix of strength and plyometric work.

citation.title: Resistance Exercise for Improving Running Economy and Running Biomechanics and Decreasing Running-Related Injury Risk: A Narrative Review
citation.authors: Suc A, Sarko P, Plesa J, Kozinc Z
citation.venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

claims.claim: Two sessions a week is enough to add strength work without crowding running, and combining heavy strength with plyometric work improves running economy and time-trial performance.
claims.evidence: A systematic review and meta-analysis found heavy resistance and plyometric training both improve running economy and time-trial performance as an adjunct to running.

citation.title: Heavy Resistance Training Versus Plyometric Training for Improving Running Economy and Running Time Trial Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation.authors: Eihara Y, Takao K, Sugiyama T, Maeo S, Terada M, Kanehisa H, Isaka T

summary_tier_a: Strength training helps runners: it improves running economy, supports good biomechanics and lowers injury risk. Multi-joint free-weight and bodyweight exercises tend to transfer to running better than machine-only work because they ask for more coordination and control, yet when load is matched, free weights and machines build strength and muscle similarly. Two sessions a week is enough, ideally mixing heavier strength with a little plyometric work. Bodyweight moves can be progressed with harder variations, slower lowering phases and longer holds when load is not available.
notes: Backs the bodyweight catalog and the equipment question in onboarding.
